Hi Joe,

In the future, when asking about a parser error please quote the error message, which in your case is:

TRANSLATING MODEL 'schools_code' FROM Stan CODE TO C++ CODE NOW.
Error in stanc(model_code = schools_code) :
  failed to parse Stan model 'schools_code' with error message:
LOCATION:  file=input; line=23, column=9
mu[i] <- beta + u2[school[i]] ;

^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

attempt to assign variable in wrong block. left-hand-side variable origin=parameter
Parser expecting: "}"

This happens because mu is defined as a (free) parameter (which cannot be assigned to), rather than a transformed parameter or a local parameter in the model section. In general, your code is essentially BUGS code, and there are some differences in the Stan language that need to be kept in mind. These include: not using periods in variable names, bounding the support of a variable instead of using a uniform prior, using the standard deviation rather than the precision in the normal distribution, vectorizing instead of looping where possible, and defining a variable before using it. Most of these are mentioned in the Appendix entitled "Stan for Users of BUGS" in the Stan manual.

I'll rewrite your code so that it parses and add some comments with //.

data {
    int<lower=1> n2 ;  
    int<lower=1> N ;
    real y[N] ;
    int school[N] ;
}

parameters {
//    real mu[N] ; // moved to model{} section

real u2[n2] ;
    real<lower=0> tau ;

//    real<lower=0> tau.u2 ;
    real<lower=0> tau_u2 ; // no periods in names
//    real beta ;
    real <lower=0,upper=1000> beta; // add bounds on the support of beta
}

model
{
    real mu; // can be scalar in this case
    real sigma;

    sigma <- sqrt(1/tau);

# Level 1 definition
    for(i in 1:N) {

mu <- beta + u2[school[i]] ;
        y[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma) ; // normal is parameterized in terms of the standard deviation
    }
    # level 2 definitions
//    for (j in 1:n2) {
//        u2[j] ~ normal(0,tau.u2) ;
//    }
    u2 ~ normal(0, sqrt(1/tau_u2)); // vectorize instead of looping where possible and use standard deviation
# Priors for fixed effects
//    beta[1] ~ uniform(0,1000) ; // not necessary when the support of beta is bounded on both sides
# Priors for random terms

// use gamma, rather than dgamma
    tau ~ gamma(0.001000,0.001000) ;
    tau_u2 ~ gamma(0.001000,0.001000) ;
}


In addition, while it is not wrong to define the tau and tau_u2 as parameters representing if you have an informative prior over a precision, it would probably be clearer to just define sigma and sigma_u2 as nonnegative parameters in the parameters {} block (and not define tau or tau_u2) and then use sigma and sigma_u2 in the model{} block (rather than defining them as local parameters as I have done).

Ben

>
> Is there anything I can do to improve the speed ? I already set CXXFLAGS to 03 in the makeconf

The main thing that would speed it up is to
vectorize the normal() calls. Even if you have to use
an intermediate array it'll be faster, but only
by a factor of 2--4 or so, not a factor
of 300.

Also, be sure to measure the effective sample size,
not just the number of draws. It's easy to generate
gazillions of Metropolis draws quickly by choosing
a small proposal scale, but the effective sample size
will be lousy.

Do you know what algorithms mlwin and MCMCglmm use
for sampling?

Stan is at a disadvantage compared to systems that can exploit
sufficient statistics or calculate posteriors analytically as
can be done for many GLMs.

We're going to focus more on this kind of GLM in the
future for speed, but there's nothing on the horizon
immediately to look forward to.

- Bob

You can also specify -march=native in CXXFLAGS, but that won't make too much of a difference.

parts:
I agree with Bob—vectorizing the normal() calls is the easiest thing
to do, and could produce a very significant speedup. That's
implemented below. Also, it's definitely not fair to just look at
iterations—not all MCMC samples are created equal.

One more way that the model could be sped up is by reparameterizing
the model so that tau_u2 and u2 are decoupled in the prior, which is
also implemented below. When you say something like

<code>
tau ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
u2[i] ~ normal(mu, 1/sqrt(tau));
</code>

the result is that
1. there is a very strong correlation in the prior (and often in the
posterior) between tau and the elements of u2, which is undesirable
because it demands small step sizes and
2. marginally u2[i] has a very, very heavy-tailed prior, which can
result in a heavy-tailed posterior, which is more difficult for
NUTS/HMC (and Gibbs, and Metropolis, and pretty much any MCMC
algorithm) to sample from.

You can instead say something like

<code>
tau ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
u2_z[i] ~ normal(mu, 1);
u2[i] <- u2_z * 1/sqrt(tau);
</code>

and sample on the space of the transformed variable u2_z instead of
u2. This prior is equivalent to the one above, but u2_z is
uncorrelated with tau (which is good) and has normal tails (which is
also good). I've found that this sort of reparameterization can
dramatically improve performance of hierarchical models.

The model as written below should give a significant speedup, I think.
(Assuming I didn't screw it up accidentally.) But again, please
remember that what counts is the quality of the samples, not the total
number of iterations.

Matt

<code>

data {
int<lower=1> n2 ;
int<lower=1> N ;
real y[N] ;
int school[N] ;
}

parameters {

real u2_z[n2] ; // drawn from a standard normal
real<lower=0> tau ;
real<lower=0> tau_u2 ; // no periods in names

real <lower=0,upper=1000> beta; // add bounds on the support of beta
}

transformed parameters {
real u2[n2]; // this is the u2 you care about

for (i in 1:n2) {
u2[i] <- u2_z[i] * sqrt(1/tau_u2);
}
}

model
{
real mu[N]; // should be vectorized

real sigma;

sigma <- sqrt(1/tau);

# Level 1 definition
for(i in 1:N) {
mu[i] <- beta + u2[school[i]] ;
// y[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma) ; // normal is parameterized in

terms of the standard deviation
}

y ~ normal(mu, sigma); // vectorize instead of looping

# level 2 definitions

u2 ~ normal(0, sqrt(1/tau_u2)); // vectorize instead of looping
where possible and use standard deviation

# Priors for random terms

// use gamma, rather than dgamma

tau ~ gamma(0.001,0.001) ;
tau_u2 ~ gamma(0.001,0.001) ;
}
</code>

I don't think I would call this model a GLM.  I would say it is a hierarchical linear model (MLM) or a linear mixed model (LMM).  One could refer to it as a generalized linear mixed model but only in the sense that all linear mixed models are also generalized linear mixed models.

I'm not sure how easy (well it is more a question of whether or not it is exceptionally difficult) it would be to extend the sampler framework to take advantage of models with a linear predictor expression like this.  Conditional on the values of sigma2 and sigma2.u2 the distribution of beta and mu is a multivariate normal and can be vectorized except that you really want to use a sparse model matrix, not a dense model matrix, when you get to large numbers of observations.

You can read up on Andrew's full set of recommendations here:

Bayesian Analysis (2006) 1, Number 3, pp. 515ï¿½533
Prior distributions for variance parameters in
hierarchical models
Andrew Gelman

http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/taumain.pdf

We've been using half-Cauchy distributions for deviations and
full Cauchy for regression coefficients. In
Stan, you don't even need to truncate because we only need
the probability up to a proportion. So you could replace this:

> tau ~ gamma(0.001, 0.001);
> u2_z[i] ~ normal(mu, 1);
> u2[i] <- u2_z * 1/sqrt(tau);

with a proper z-score and a prior directly on deviation:

sigma ~ cauchy(0,5);
u2_z[i] ~ normal(0,1);
u2[i] <- mu + u2_z[i] * sigma;

I also pulled mu out for reasons Matt outlined in previous
messages (and which is going into the next manual).

Because Stan doesn't exploit conjugacy, the Cauchy will
be roughly the same efficiency per iteration as the gamma
prior.

Our standard advice to do some sensitivity analysis also
stands -- if you don't want the prior to have a big effect,
make sure it doesn't by testing alternatives.

- Bob

The default in Stan is to adapt step size during warmup,
but then to use a fixed step size in sampling. So you
see the same step size in every sample.

If you use the varying step command-line flag, epsilon_pm,
you get different step sizes per iteration. The "_pm" is
missing from the doc in the manual, so I just fixed that.

Model execution option (page 23 or so of the manual):

--epsilon_pm=<[0,1]>
Sample epsilon uniformly from the interval
[epsilon * (1 - epsilon_pm), epsilon * (1 + epsilon_pm)]
(default = 0.0)


- Bob

Never mind about that hypothesis I mentioned.

The reason for the slow mixing we're seeing is pretty basic—in this
model, the intercept beta (just out of curiosity—why call it beta
instead of alpha?) is very highly anti-correlated with the
school-level effects u2. On average, the posterior correlation is
around -0.9. So that's the source of the slow mixing.

One way around this is to sample from the coefficient vector, which in this case can be orthogonalized.  In general the conditional distribution of coefficients, even in the case of mixed-effects models can be orthogonalized.

IIRC JAGS has a specialized sampler for this.

I'm not sure how difficult it would be but the ability to use sparse matrices, which are supported in Eigen and RcppEigen, would be very helpful here.

For the record, I would use something like
library(lme4)
library(rstan)

set.seed(1234321)
samp <- within(data.frame(schoolID=gl(300,100)),
               outcome <- 20 + rnorm(30000, sd=10) + rnorm(300,sd=5)[schoolID])
(lm1 <- lmer(outcome ~ 1|schoolID, samp))
## The next line can only be run with the development lme4 installed as
## install.packages("lme4", repos="http://R-forge.R-project.org")
densityplot(pr1 <- profile(lm1), ylab=NULL, layout=c(3,1))

schools_code <- '
  data {
    int<lower=1> N;                   // number of observations
    int<lower=1> J;                   // number of schools
    int<lower=1,upper=J> school[N];   // school for each obs
    real         y[N];          // observed outcome
  }
  parameters {
    real mu; 
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0> sigma1;
    real eta[J];
  }
  model {
    real mm[N];
for (i in 1:N)

mm[i] <- mu + eta[school[i]];

    y   ~ normal(mm, sigma);
    eta ~ normal(0, sigma1);

    sigma ~ gamma(0.001000,0.001000) ;
    sigma1 ~ gamma(0.001000,0.001000) ;
  }
'

fit <- stan(model_name="schools", model_code=schools_code,
            data=with(samp, list(N=nrow(samp), J=length(levels(schoolID)),
            y=outcome, school=as.integer(schoolID))),
            iter = 1000, chains = 4)
